source.title: Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining
source.authors: Angela Tang; V. Anand; Gonçalo Paulo

page_placements.theme: Scope of the transferred trait: target-specific, preference contexts, semantic coherence
Sender and receiver properties moderate transfer

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests subliminal preference transfer and reports transfer across different base models, challenging the proposed same-base requirement while refining the account of what carries the signal.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports many teacher/student hyperparameter sweeps and cross-checkpoint grids. Rows below focus on separately reported outcomes bearing on the claim versions; cited results from other papers are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own subliminal-transfer experiments on Pythia, PolyPythia and DataDecide OLMo base models. It uses filtered-number hard labels and on-policy soft labels. It reports transfer when teacher and student differ in initialization, data order, corpus, size and architecture, which argues directly against B. It also tests what carries the signal (D) and robustness to full fine-tuning and held-out prompts (E). The setting differs from the original (base models rather than chat models, plus a new soft-label route), so T2/T3 elements are present, but the central contribution is a challenge and restatement of B and D.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that shared initialization, data order, corpus, size or architecture are not required for transfer, though a shared base often strengthens hard-label transfer at the evaluated endpoints. They find that sending and receiving abilities develop separately during pretraining, producing asymmetry. Number frequencies alone carry much of the hard-label signal in Pythia (less in OLMo), and animal-token probabilities carry much of the top-K soft-label signal. Neither LoRA nor adaptive optimizers are required, and soft-label distillation transfers more consistently with less training.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts the original hard-label filtered-number pipeline from instruction-tuned chat models to pretrained base models and adds on-policy soft-label distillation, synthetic-document teacher tuning, and independently resampled number-frequency tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer depends on teacher fine-tuning settings, student training duration, optimizer and learning rate, teacher document wording/position/density, model/checkpoint and teacher–student direction. Same-model transfer can peak and decline; top-K choice changes transfer and language-modeling cost. Removing in-context number examples roughly halves hard-label transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: Transfer is target-specific: non-target animals fall slightly. Off-topic prompts show only a 0.018 gain vs 0.29–0.47 on preference prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminally transferred preferences are specific to the target and largely confined to preference contexts.

fits_no_version.finding: The abilities to transmit and to acquire a preference develop separately over pretraining. Cross-model transfer is asymmetric when roles are reversed, and a product of teacher and student factors explains 90–97% of held-out cross-checkpoint variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transfer strength factorizes into sender and receiver capacities that emerge at different pretraining stages.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be uploaded.
record.problems: Much of the detailed evidence uses small base models, especially Pythia-160M. Strong hard-label effects can involve extended student training and language-modeling degradation. Resampling comparisons differ in traits and training settings across Pythia and OLMo. The authors note that animal-token removal may leave semantically related tokens, and that their trait coverage is narrow.
record.rows_left_out: Not exhaustive: omitted many separately plotted hyperparameter sweeps, checkpoint-to-checkpoint cells, number-sequence construction variants, and individual cross-model pairs. Main omitted locations include Figures 2, 4–5, A3–A9, A11–A18, A25–A43 and Tables A8–A16; rows were limited to the principal reported outcomes for the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning data types; instruction-tuned chat models (only base models are tested); traits beyond animal, tree and colour preferences.
Most large cross-family pairs under hard labels; only Pythia↔OLMo-1B is tested across architectures there.
All of it; no misalignment or harmful-trait transfer experiment.
Divergence-token and gradient/shared-initialization theoretical accounts are not directly tested. The steering-vector account is probed only as a predictor.
Other student LoRA ranks (the student rank is fixed at 8; only teacher ranks are swept); full fine-tuning in the soft-label setting.
All of it; no prompt-only intervention.

missing.what: Soft-label cross-size and cross-family transfer: 26 of 30 different-model pairs transfer, including Pythia↔AMD-OLMo-1B and Qwen2.5↔Qwen3. Teachers of 1B+ into Pythia-160M barely move it.

Hard-label 160M↔410M with different data order: 20.2% and 10.9% exceed the control maximum (nulls 4.9%, 4.8%). OLMo same-model 86.4%, same init/different corpus 37.4%, different init/same corpus 47.7%.
Same-model vs mismatched condition comparisons: Pythia mean Δ difference 0.38–0.46 for dog. OLMo same-model exceeds cross-corpus by Δ 0.083–0.094.
Same init, data order and hyperparameters but a different hardware/software stack (Rerun1234) reduces transfer to about the level of different data order.
Lion, different init/same data order: not significant (p=0.057). Three Dolma1.7-sender OLMo arms are not individually significant.
Steerability's rank correlation with transfer (0.796) vanishes after controlling for teacher preference (partial r = −0.10). This bears on the steering-vector account.
missing.locator: Appendix A.7, Table A4, Figure A4

missing.what: Permuting frequency mass among same-digit numbers (Pall) drops transfer to near control in 5 of 6 comparisons: number identity matters. Splicing out in-context numbers roughly halves transfer.
Tree and colour preferences transfer under both hard and soft labels in Pythia-160M.
Same-model soft-label transfer from preference-prompt and SDF teachers; about 5,000 samples already give median gains of 0.09–0.31.

record.verdict_notes: Record version ids (V1, V2, V4, V5) were mapped to A, B, D, E. The biggest row error: R7–R9 describe hard-label dog experiments (Table A11), not on-policy soft-label bear. Rows R11–R20 test mechanism (D), not transmission (A). The study is not an original source. Most detailed evidence comes from 160M–1B base models. Strong hard-label cross-model effects often need extended student training with LM degradation.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests animal preferences, plus tree and color preferences in a small extension; it does not test every possible trait or all listed data types such as code and maths reasoning.
It tests multiple initialization, data-order, corpus, size, and architecture relationships, not every possible pair of different base models.
No harmful trait or misalignment transfer experiment is reported.
The study tests number-frequency resampling and removal of animal-name tokens from a loss; it does not establish a complete mechanism or directly test divergence-token or gradient-alignment accounts.
It tests full fine-tuning with SGD and AdamW, and evaluates on held-out preference prompts. It does not report an isolated result for each student LoRA rank.
No prompt-only intervention without fine-tuning is tested.
